newsitem.title: USA: Dlr starts mixed in US, EMU delay fears cool a bit.
newsitem.headline: Dlr starts mixed in US, EMU delay fears cool a bit.

text.p: The dollar started mixed in the U.S., with dollar/yen opening softer as the market discounted a rising Japanese trade surplus before Japan's current account data due later on Tuesday.
But the greenback reclaimed 1.71 marks overnight while the market pondered whether French foot dragging equaled delay in Europe's planned single currency.

Analysts said a tough negotiating stance on the stability pact by the new French government should not lead to an assumption the rigid terms of the Maastricht Treaty would be fiddled with or the the euro's launch would be postponed.

"My take on it is the French are negotiators. The new government is trying to eke out as many concessions from Europe as they can," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Whether they ratify a stability pact in Amsterdam next week or not is "immaterial", Chandler said, as long as European leaders continue to stress the tough budget criteria must not be fudged and will be adhered to, as German Finance Minister Theo Waigel did on Tuesday.
Dollar/mark opened at 1.7125/35, up from 1.7065/75 at Monday's close and at 112.45/50 yen, off from 112.90/00.

Waigel, after a meeting of the Christian Democrats' parliamentary faction, said it was important for Germany to meet the budget deficit condition for monetary union and that talking about loosening of the 3.0 percent target was risky because it would arouse expectations in other countries.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel helped assuage fears of an EMU delay on Tuesday, saying France's call for time to examine the pact to control deficits after the planned 1999 euro debut would not hamstring plans for the whole project.
Traders said they are prepared to weather a thickening barrage of comments from European officials as EMU approaches.
Jim Powers, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at West Deutsche Landesbank Girozentrale, said a lot of comments are starting to fall on deaf ears as the market filters out new from old.
"You've got to dissect what hasn't been said already. You've got to take everything and analyze it before you want to act on it," he said.

Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson added his voice to the chorus Tuesday, saying that although he expected the stability pact to be signed at the European Union summit on Monday and Tuesday in Amsterdam, there could be some delay.
Persson also said he expects monetary union to kick off as planned in 1999.

Against the yen, the dollar overnight moved off highs reached after Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka called recent forex moves excessive and said Japan will deal appropriately with excessive forex swings.
The dollar was capped in Tokyo by exporter offers and hedge selling interest by Japanese trust banks, dealers said.
But the market was mostly on hold before the 1950 EDT/2350 GMT release of data on Japan's April current account surplus, which is expected to have widened from the year-ago period.
A Reuters poll of economists showed, on average, that the April current account surplus would grow to 1.13 trillion yen, compared with a surplus of 566.6 billion yen last year.
A wider-than-expected surplus would come at a particularly awkward time, and could continue to weigh on dollar/yen before the Group of Seven meeting in Denver on June 20-22, dealers said.

Elsewhere, dollar/Swiss opened at 1.4415/25, up from 1.4370/80 but the dollar fell to Canadian $1.3865/70 from C$1.3882/87. The pound rose to $1.6383/93 from $1.6368/78 and the Australian dollar rose to $0.7622/27 from $0.7615/20.
((--Alden Bentley, 212 859 1667))
